'''Bertrand I. Halperin''' (born December 6, 1941) is an American physicist, former holder of the [[Hollis Chair of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy|Hollis Chair of Mathematicks and Natural Philosophy]] at the [[physics]] department of [[Harvard University]].<ref name="AIP_biography">{{Cite web |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11506020.html |title=Halperin, Bertrand I.  |publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]]  |access-date=January 7, 2019}}</ref> In 2006, he received the [[Wolf Prize in Physics]] for his various contribution to [[condensed matter physics]], including work on  [[KTHNY theory]] for two-dimensional melting.

== Biography==
Bertrand Halperin was born in [[Brooklyn, New York]], where he grew up in the [[Crown Heights, Brooklyn|Crown Heights]] neighborhood and attended public schools. His mother was Eva Teplitzky Halperin and his father Morris Halperin. His mother was a college administrator and his father a customs inspector.<ref name="Halperin">{{cite journal |last1=Halperin |first1=Bertrand I. |title=A Career in Physics |journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics |date=10 March 2021 |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=15–28 |doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-060120-092219 |bibcode=2021ARCMP..12...15H |s2cid=228892037 |issn=1947-5454|doi-access=free }}</ref> Both his parents were born in [[USSR]]. His paternal grandmother's family the Maximovs claimed descent from [[Baal Shem Tov|Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov]] (BeShT).{{Cn|date=October 2024}}

He attended [[Harvard University]] (class of 1961),<ref name="Halperin"/> and did his graduate work at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], with [[John J. Hopfield]] (PhD 1965).<ref name="AIP_biography"/> 
==Scientific career==
After working at [[Bell Laboratories]] for 10 years (1966–1976), Murray Hill, New Jersey he was appointed professor of physics at [[Harvard University]].

In the 1970s, he, together with [[David Robert Nelson]], worked out a theory of two-dimensional [[melting]], predicting the [[hexatic phase]] before it was experimentally observed by Pindak ''et al.'' In the 1980s, he made contributions to the theory of the [[quantum Hall effect]] and of the [[fractional quantum Hall effect]]. His recent interests lie in the area of strongly interacting low-dimensional electron systems.<ref name="<aps2019" />

== Awards and recognition==
Halperin was elected a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1972,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1972&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellows Archive|publisher=APS|access-date= 4 October 2020}}</ref> a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1981,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bertrand Israel Halperin |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/bertrand-israel-halperin |access-date=2022-04-19 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref> a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1982,<ref name="NAS">{{Cite web |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/bertrand-i-halperin-whopnd/ |title=Bertrand Halperin |work=NAS Member Directory  |access-date=January 7, 2019}}</ref> and a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Bertrand+Halperin&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-04-19 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> In 2001, he was awarded the [[Lars Onsager Prize]].<ref name="Onsager2001">{{Cite web |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Halperin&first_nm=Bertrand&year=2001 |title=2001 Lars Onsager Prize Recipient |publisher=APS Physics |quote="For his wide-ranging contributions to statistical physics and quantum fluids, especially the elucidation of the quantum Hall effect and other low-dimensional electronic phenomena; and for his exemplary leadership in bringing theory to bear on the understanding of experiments."  |access-date=January 7, 2019}}</ref> In 2003, he was awarded the [[Wolf Prize]] in physics for his work on "two- dimensional melting, disordered systems and strongly interacting electrons", the other half went to [[Anthony James Leggett]].<ref name="Wolf2003">{{Cite web |url=https://www.haaretz.com/1.4824351 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190108202230/https://www.haaretz.com/1.4824351 |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 8, 2019 |title=Multinational Winners of Wolf Prizes for Mathematics, Physics and Agriculture |last=Sa'ar |first=Relly |work=Haaretz |quote=This year's Wolf Prize for physics will be awarded to Professor Bertrand Halperin of Harvard University and Professor Anthony Leggett of Illinois University. The jury said the prize was in recognition of the researchers' contribution to the field of condensed matter theory. Halperin, 61, is a member of the National Academy of Sciences and has been a professor at Harvard since 1976. |date=January 15, 2003 |access-date=January 7, 2019}}</ref> In 2016 he was [[Lise Meitner Distinguished Lecture]]r.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theophys.kth.se/~egor/LiseMeitnerLecture.html|title=LiseMeitnerLecture|access-date=2019-06-19|archive-date=2016-06-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160611054853/http://www.theophys.kth.se/~egor/LiseMeitnerLecture.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2018, he was awarded the 2019 [[List of American Physical Society prizes and awards|APS Medal for Exceptional Achievement in Research]],<ref name="<aps2019"> {{Cite web |url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201808/medal.cfm |title=2019 APS Medal for Exceptional Achievement in Research Awarded to Bertrand I. Halperin  |work=APS News |quote=Among his many honors, Halperin is a member of the National Academy of Sciences and the American Philosophical Society, and a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In addition to his APS awards, he received the Dannie Heineman Prize of the Göttingen Akademie der Wissenschaften, the Lars Onsager Lecture and Medal of the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, an honorary doctorate from the Weizmann Institute of Science, the Lise Meitner Lecture and Medal, and the Wolf Prize in Physics. |date=2018 |access-date=January 7, 2019}}</ref> for "his seminal contributions to theoretical condensed matter physics, especially his pioneering work on the role of topology in both classical and quantum systems."<ref>[https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Halperin&first_nm=Bertrand&year=2019 "2019 APS Medal for Exceptional Achievement in Research Recipient: Bertrand I. Halperin"]</ref>
